mappings.note: The conclusion asked for is the classification of blood as a colloid (LO-14), but the three clues supplied are that filtration fails, that centrifugation works and that the cells are invisible -- which is LO-13's sentence almost verbatim. Both cited because the evidence and the verdict belong to different outcomes.

Reads a sublimation apparatus backwards to pick which pair it suits -- LO-12's 'uses sublimation to separate a suitable solid mixture'. The three wrong options are pairs with no sublimable component, so sublimability is the assessed idea.
Places colloid particles on the 1-1000 nm band between solutions and suspensions -- LO-14's particle-size clause, stated numerically. No light test, so not LO-15.

Assertion and reason together are LO-14's 'explains why the particles of a colloid do not settle', with molecular bombardment as the mechanism. Contrast with the muddy-water assertion-reason item, which is the same outcome seen from the suspension side.
Names the phenomenon: Tyndall effect, against refraction and total internal reflection. LO-15's demonstration clause reduced to the term itself.

The thermometer reading 56 degrees fixes what is in the condenser -- boiling-point-driven separation, LO-10. The item turns on which component boils first, not on the apparatus names, so it stays with LO-10 rather than a generic inquiry code.

Picks sunbeams through forest leaves as the everyday Tyndall case, rejecting dissolving, boiling and precipitation. LO-15. The other Tyndall items use a laser in the lab; this one transfers the same outcome to an outdoor observation.
Asks for the term 'dispersed phase', which LO-15 names explicitly alongside dispersion medium. Not LO-14: no size band is involved, only the vocabulary of colloid structure.

Ordering the steps that make a stable oil-water-soap emulsion. LO-15 is the only outcome mentioning emulsions, so it is the home, though its wording is 'recognising an emulsion as a liquid colloid' and this item asks the student to make one -- a mild stretch, recorded. Not LO-16: nothing is being separated.
Classifies milk and vanishing cream as oil-in-water emulsions, which is LO-15's emulsion clause combined with naming which liquid is dispersed and which is the medium.

Proteins as emulsifying agents keeping milk from separating -- the stability of a liquid colloid, LO-15's emulsion clause. Not LO-13: the coagulation distractor is the wrong answer here, and nothing is being separated or clumped.

Statement 3 (colloids look homogeneous but are not) and the false statement 2 (suspensions transparent and unfilterable) are both LO-14 property comparisons; statement 1 is the non-scattering of true solutions, which is LO-15. Two codes because the item cannot be answered from either alone.

Three components, four steps, and the whole item is whether sublimation comes before the water is added -- LO-16's 'justifies the order chosen'. Same outcome as the part-1 figure-based version of this mixture; the family genuinely shares one outcome because LO-16 is written for exactly this task.
Sewage treatment clumping fine waste particles is coagulation, named in LO-13 as the alternative when particles are too fine to filter. Industrial setting rather than the alum beaker, same outcome.
Bare definition of a homogeneous mixture -- LO-6. Two marks, no classification list, no particle size.

One difference by appearance is LO-6's 'distinguishes a homogeneous from a heterogeneous mixture by observation' -- the by-observation clause specifically, which is what separates it from the particle-size route in LO-14.

Asks for an everyday heterogeneous example -- LO-6's 'classifies everyday mixtures'. Sand in water is offered as a settling, visible mixture, which is classification by observation rather than by the 1000 nm threshold.

Defines concentration as amount of solute per amount of solvent or solution. LO-7 is the concentration outcome; it is written around calculation, and this item stops at the definition that underpins it.

POOR FIT, second instance of the same gap. The formula asked for is mass by VOLUME percentage, which LO-7 does not list -- it names only mass by mass and volume by volume. Cited as nearest because no other code touches concentration, but curriculum 82 has no outcome for % m/V.
The general solid-in-liquid solubility-versus-temperature relationship -- LO-8's temperature clause, stated without any curve or table.

Why the definition of a saturated solution has to name a temperature. This joins LO-8's two clauses -- the saturation definition and the temperature dependence -- and is the sharpest single item on that link.

Bare definition of a saturated solution -- the first clause of LO-8. Kept separate in intent from the preceding item, which asks why the temperature qualifier is needed rather than what the term means.

The principle of purification by crystallisation, answered as differing solubility at different temperatures -- LO-9's 'explains the principle of crystallisation'. Family rule kept: no solubility figure or curve is read here, so this stays on LO-9 rather than LO-8, which owns data reading.
Slow cooling of copper sulfate gives large, well-shaped crystals -- LO-9's slow-cooling clause plus the regular-solid description, in the single most direct item on it.
An application of simple distillation, answered by restating its condition -- miscible liquids with a large boiling-point gap. LO-10's appropriateness clause.
